senses.definition: To explain something already said or written by laying out the reasoning behind it.
senses.caution: It is formal and can sound stiff out loud. Asking someone to elucidate says they were unclear, so use it about a document rather than about the person who wrote it.
senses.example: The deck lands the recommendation but never elucidates how we got to that number, and that is the part the committee will push on.

cues.text: A steering committee accepts your recommendation but says the reasoning behind one number is a black box. You are writing back to promise the appendix will open it up.
A colleague's design doc states a decision without showing the trade-off behind it, and in review you want to ask them to bring that reasoning into the open.
Your father repeats the conclusion of a health article without any of what it argued, and you want him to take you through the actual case it made.
A book group is stuck on a chapter that one member plainly understood, and you want to invite them to open it up for everyone.

distractors: To make something deliberately hard to follow so the plain version stays out of reach.
To go back over a draft and tighten the phrasing without changing what it says.
To back a claim with evidence that someone else can go and check for themselves.
To put right something that was wrong, such as an error, an imbalance, or a missed duty.
To ask someone to talk through what they have learned, informally and without an agenda.
